ei.title: Two Heroes Who Fought a Deadly Disease
ei.subject: 영어2

fullPassage: One evening in late November 1932, a bitterly cold wind blows fiercely as two figures emerge from a laboratory. Darkness begins to fall as they set out into a world of failed banks, collapsed industry, and widespread despair — a world ruined by three years of the Great Depression. The workday has come to an end, but for Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering, a different kind of work is about to begin. They are on their way to visit the homes of children suffering from a deadly disease called pertussis*. The two women go from home to home collecting samples from the sick children by the faint light of their lamps. They listen to the tragic stories of desperate and unemployed parents as the children, coughing uncontrollably and struggling to breathe, barely hold on to life. Pertussis is a bacterial disease characterized by serious coughing, breathing difficulties, and the high-pitched “whooping” sound that people with the disease make as they try to breathe in. Because of this distinct sound, people started to call the disease “whooping cough.” For a long time, this terrible illness was one of the greatest terrors of families with young children, because babies who contracted it had a high chance of dying. In the 1930s, an average of 6,000 people died of whooping cough in the United States each year. Ninety-five percent of them were children under five years of age. The cause of the disease had been identified in 1906, but the vaccines that had been developed were ineffective. Scientists and researchers worked for more than 20 years to produce an effective one, but their efforts were fruitless — until Kendrick and Eldering came along. Pearl Kendrick studied bacteriology in university and was recruited by the Michigan Department of Health in 1920. It was there that she met fellow bacteriologist Grace Eldering. The two quickly bonded, and in 1932 they started working together on a vaccine for whooping cough. Personal experience served as motivation for both of them, as they had each survived whooping cough as children themselves and remembered the severe pain of the disease. Both scientists were also eager to promote children’s health. Unfortunately, research funding was extremely limited due to the Great Depression. Also, Kendrick and Eldering had to develop the vaccine as a side project. It was like having a second job for which they never received any payment. Still, when they finished their normal duties each day, they would get started on the work that they were enthusiastic about. The difficulties they faced did not stop them from persisting toward their goal. They did not do the work to make extra money; instead, they worked to relieve the suffering of innocent children and their families. They began the process of developing their vaccine by gathering samples of the bacteria that cause whooping cough. To support them, local doctors and nurses provided “cough plates” from their patients. The patients coughed onto a petri dish*, which was then put into an incubator. This allowed the bacteria to grow into colonies that Kendrick and Eldering could analyze. When they collected samples on their own, they would go to the homes of sick children. Each time, they were reminded once again of the dreadful suffering caused by the disease. The sight of these innocent young victims coughing and struggling to breathe was a powerful reminder of the urgent need for an effective vaccine. Kendrick and Eldering spent many long nights studying the bacteria and finally produced a potential vaccine. Before they performed any clinical trials, though, they had to be certain that it would not have any negative side effects on the subjects. They ran many laboratory tests, and they even injected it into themselves to confirm that it was safe. From 1934 to 1935, they conducted their first field test with 1,592 children. In the group of 712 vaccinated children, only four developed whooping cough, and none of these cases were serious. Despite the apparent success of the vaccine, Kendrick and Eldering wanted further confirmation of its effectiveness. They became determined to expand their research and run more tests with larger groups of children. However, they were unable to proceed because they were facing a severe lack of funds. With thousands of children continuing to suffer from the disease, they found themselves in a desperate situation. Luckily, they got help from an unexpected figure. In 1936, First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt herself visited the laboratory and saw with her own eyes the efforts that Kendrick and Eldering were making in their battle against whooping cough. Eleanor Roosevelt, whose husband suffered from polio*, was interested in fighting infectious diseases. She spent time with the women and came to realize the enormous importance of their work. With her help, Kendrick and Eldering were able to secure enough funding to conduct a large-scale trial. By 1937, Kendrick and Eldering were able to include more than 4,200 children in their trial. Just as in their first field test, the vaccinated group demonstrated a high level of immunity against the disease. The scientific community was amazed at the results, and, in 1940, the vaccine started being distributed all across the United States. Four years later, it was added to the American Medical Association’s list of recommended immunizations, and soon after, there was a dramatic decline in whooping cough infections. In the mid-1970s, the number of annual deaths caused by whooping cough, which had reached 7,518 in 1934, dropped to under 10. Kendrick and Eldering were often told that they could have become very wealthy if they had patented their vaccine. However, they replied that it had not been created by them alone, but with the help of many others. They also avoided personal interviews, not wanting to reveal the great contribution they had made. They said that they had genuinely enjoyed the challenge of creating the vaccine, so the excessive praise that they received made them uncomfortable. In the end, knowing that so many lives were being saved thanks to their hard work was enough of a reward for these remarkable and modest heroes.

questions.passage: They are on their way to visit the homes of children suffering from a (A)[deadly / harmless] disease called pertussis*. The two women go from home to home collecting samples from the sick children by the faint light of their lamps. They listen to the (B)[tragic / joyful] stories of desperate and unemployed parents as the children, coughing uncontrollably and struggling to breathe, barely hold on to life. Pertussis is a bacterial disease characterized by serious coughing, breathing difficulties, and the high-pitched “whooping” sound that people with the disease make as they try to breathe in. Because of this distinct sound, people started to call the disease “whooping cough. ” For a long time, this (C)[terrible / wonderful] illness was one of the greatest terrors of families with young children, because babies who contracted it had a high chance of dying.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 (A), (B), (C)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① deadly(치명적인)+tragic(비극적인)+terrible(끔찍한): 아이들이 앓는 치명적 질병, 부모들의 비극적 이야기, 끔찍한 병이라는 문맥에 모두 맞음 ← 정답
❌ ② harmless(무해한)는 치명적 질병과 정반대
❌ ③ joyful(즐거운)은 비극적 이야기와 정반대
❌ ④ wonderful(멋진)은 끔찍한 병과 정반대
det.tip: deadly=치명적인, tragic=비극적인, terrible=끔찍한

questions.passage: Personal experience served as motivation for both of them, as they had each survived whooping cough as children themselves and remembered the severe pain of the disease. Both scientists were also (A)[eager / reluctant] to promote children’s health. Unfortunately, research funding was extremely (B)[limited / abundant] due to the Great Depression. Also, Kendrick and Eldering had to develop the vaccine as a side project. It was like having a second job for which they never received any payment. Still, when they finished their normal duties each day, they would get started on the work that they were (C)[enthusiastic / indifferent] about.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 (A), (B), (C)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① reluctant(마지못한)는 아동 건강을 열망한 문맥과 반대
✅ ② eager(열망하는)+limited(제한된)+enthusiastic(열정적인): 아동 건강 증진을 열망했고, 연구 자금은 제한적이었으며, 열정을 쏟은 일이라는 문맥에 맞음 ← 정답
❌ ③ abundant(풍부한)는 자금이 제한적이었다는 문맥과 반대
❌ ④ indifferent(무관심한)는 열정적이었다는 문맥과 반대
det.tip: eager=열망하는, limited=제한된, enthusiastic=열정적인

questions.passage: Kendrick and Eldering spent many long nights studying the bacteria and finally produced a (A)[potential / proven] vaccine. Before they performed any clinical trials, though, they had to be certain that it would not have any (B)[negative / positive] side effects on the subjects. They ran many laboratory tests, and they even injected it into themselves to confirm that it was (C)[safe / harmful]. From 1934 to 1935, they conducted their first field test with 1,592 children. In the group of 712 vaccinated children, only four developed whooping cough, and none of these cases were serious.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 (A), (B), (C)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① proven(입증된)은 아직 시험 전 단계인 '잠재적' 백신 문맥과 반대
❌ ② positive(긍정적인)는 '부작용이 없어야 한다'는 문맥에서 negative(부정적인)여야 함
❌ ③ harmful(해로운)은 스스로 주사해 '안전한지' 확인한 문맥과 반대
✅ ④ potential(잠재적인)+negative(부정적인)+safe(안전한): 가능성 있는 백신, 부정적 부작용, 안전 확인이라는 문맥에 맞음 ← 정답
det.tip: potential=잠재적인, negative side effects=부정적 부작용, safe=안전한

questions.passage: In the 1930s, an average of 6,000 people ①<u>died</u> of whooping cough in the United States each year.  Ninety-five percent of them were children under five years of age.  The cause of the disease had been identified in 1906, but the vaccines that had been developed were ②<u>ineffective</u>.  Scientists and researchers worked for more than 20 years to produce an ③<u>effective</u> one, but their efforts were fruitless — until Kendrick and Eldering came along.  Pearl Kendrick studied bacteriology in university and was ④<u>fired</u> by the Michigan Department of Health in 1920.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① died: 매년 6,000명이 사망했다는 문맥에 적절
✅ ② ineffective: 개발된 백신들이 효과가 없었다는 문맥에 적절
✅ ③ effective: 효과적인 백신을 만들려 했다는 문맥에 적절
❌ ④ fired(해고된) → recruited(채용된): Pearl Kendrick이 보건부에서 일을 시작한 문맥이므로 채용되었다가 맞음 ← 정답
det.tip: recruited(채용하다) ↔ fired(해고하다)

questions.passage: The difficulties they faced did not stop them from ①<u>persisting</u> toward their goal.  They did not do the work to make extra money; instead, they worked to ②<u>worsen</u> the suffering of innocent children and their families.  They began the process of developing their vaccine by ③<u>gathering</u> samples of the bacteria that cause whooping cough.  To ④<u>support</u> them, local doctors and nurses provided “cough plates” from their patients.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: ② worsen → relieve: 아이들의 고통을 덜어 주기(relieve) 위해 일했다
det.analysis:
✅ ① persisting: 목표를 향해 끈질기게 밀고 나갔다는 문맥에 적절
❌ ② worsen(악화시키다) → relieve(덜어 주다): 죄 없는 아이들의 고통을 '덜어 주려' 일했다는 문맥이므로 relieve가 맞음 ← 정답
✅ ③ gathering: 세균 표본을 모으며 백신 개발을 시작했다는 문맥에 적절
✅ ④ support: 지역 의사와 간호사가 도움을 주었다는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: relieve(덜어 주다) ↔ worsen(악화시키다)

questions.passage: Despite the apparent ①<u>success</u> of the vaccine, Kendrick and Eldering wanted further confirmation of its effectiveness.  They became determined to ②<u>expand</u> their research and run more tests with larger groups of children.  However, they were unable to proceed because they were facing a severe ③<u>abundance</u> of funds.  With thousands of children continuing to suffer from the disease, they found themselves in a desperate situation.  Luckily, they got help from an ④<u>unexpected</u> figure.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: ③ abundance → lack: 심각한 자금 부족(lack)에 직면했다
det.analysis:
✅ ① success: 백신의 명백한 성공에도 불구하고라는 문맥에 적절
✅ ② expand: 연구를 확장하기로 결심했다는 문맥에 적절
❌ ③ abundance(풍부함) → lack(부족): 연구를 진행할 수 없었던 이유가 '심각한 자금 부족'이므로 lack이 맞음 ← 정답
✅ ④ unexpected: 예상치 못한 인물에게서 도움을 받았다는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: lack(부족) ↔ abundance(풍부함)

questions.passage: They are on their way to visit the homes of children suffering from a deadly disease called pertussis*.  The two women go from home to home collecting samples from the sick children by the __________ light of their lamps. questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① faint(희미한): 어둠이 내리는 저녁, 램프의 '희미한' 빛에 의지해 표본을 모았다는 문맥에 적절 ← 정답
❌ ② bright(밝은): 램프 하나의 빛이라는 어두운 상황과 어울리지 않음
❌ ③ warm(따뜻한): 빛의 밝기를 나타내지 못함
❌ ④ electric(전기의): 1932년 가정 방문 상황, 램프 불빛이라는 단서와 맞지 않음
det.tip: by the faint light of their lamps: 램프의 희미한 빛에 의지해

det.analysis:
❌ ① parties(파티): 백신 안전성 확인 문맥과 무관
❌ ② meals(식사): 실험 상황과 무관
✅ ③ tests(검사): 많은 실험실 '검사'를 하고 스스로 주사해 안전성을 확인했다는 문맥에 적절 ← 정답
❌ ④ songs(노래): 문맥과 전혀 무관
det.tip: ran many laboratory tests: 많은 실험실 검사를 시행했다

det.analysis:
✅ ① immunity(면역력): 백신을 맞은 집단이 질병에 대해 높은 수준의 '면역력'을 보였다는 문맥에 적절 ← 정답
❌ ② danger(위험): 백신의 효과를 설명하는 흐름과 반대
❌ ③ interest(흥미): 질병에 대한 면역과 무관
❌ ④ noise(소음): 문맥과 전혀 무관
det.tip: a high level of immunity against the disease: 질병에 대한 높은 면역력

✅ ④ intensely: 맹렬히, 강렬하게 ← 정답
det.tip: fiercely = intensely = 맹렬히 (몹시 차가운 바람이 세차게 분다)

questions.passage:
(A) Before the scientists could sell the new medicine, they had to run a careful clinical <u>trial</u>. They gave the drug to many volunteers and watched them closely for several months.
(B) The man was finally proven innocent at his <u>trial</u> in court. The judge and the jury listened to all of the evidence before reaching a decision.
questions.stem: 다음 (A), (B) 두 문장에서 밑줄 친 trial의 의미로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① (A) clinical trial은 약을 자원자에게 주고 몇 달간 관찰하는 '임상 실험(시험)'을 뜻함, (B) trial in court는 판사와 배심원이 증거를 듣는 '재판'을 뜻함 ← 정답
❌ ② (A)는 재판이 아니라 실험
❌ ③ (A)는 단순한 '시도'가 아니라 의학적 실험
❌ ④ (B)는 시도가 아니라 재판
det.tip: trial: (A) (임상)실험 / (B) 재판

questions.stem:
다음 영영 정의에 해당하는 단어로 가장 적절한 것은?

"a substance that is given to people or animals to protect them from a particular disease"

det.analysis:
❌ ① bacteria: 세균 (질병을 일으키는 미생물)
✅ ② vaccine: 백신 (질병으로부터 몸을 보호하기 위해 주는 물질) ← 정답
❌ ③ symptom: 증상 (병의 겉으로 드러나는 신호)
❌ ④ patient: 환자 (병을 앓는 사람)
det.tip: vaccine = 질병으로부터 보호하기 위해 주는 물질, 즉 백신

questions.passage: They are on their way to visit the homes of children suffering from a deadly disease called pertussis*.  The two women go from home to home collecting samples from the sick children by the faint light of their lamps.  They listen to the tragic stories of desperate and unemployed parents as the children, coughing uncontrollably and struggling to breathe, barely __________.  Pertussis is a bacterial disease characterized by serious coughing, breathing difficulties, and the high-pitched “whooping” sound that people with the disease make as they try to breathe in.  Because of this distinct sound, people started to call the disease “whooping cough. ” For a long time, this terrible illness was one of the greatest terrors of families with young children, because babies who contracted it had a high chance of dying.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① give up their jobs(일을 그만두다): 아픈 아이들의 상황과 무관
❌ ② run away quickly(빨리 도망치다): 숨쉬기도 힘든 아이들 상황과 맞지 않음
❌ ③ sing out loud(큰 소리로 노래하다): 기침으로 숨을 못 쉬는 문맥과 정반대
✅ ④ hold on to life(간신히 목숨을 부지하다): 걷잡을 수 없이 기침하며 숨쉬기 힘들어하는 아이들이 겨우 목숨을 붙들고 있다는 문맥에 적절 ← 정답
det.tip: barely hold on to life: 간신히 목숨을 부지하다

questions.passage: In the 1930s, an average of 6,000 people died of whooping cough in the United States each year.  Ninety-five percent of them were children under five years of age.  The cause of the disease had been identified in 1906, but the vaccines that had been developed were ineffective.  Scientists and researchers worked for more than 20 years to produce an effective one, but their efforts were fruitless — until Kendrick and Eldering __________.  Pearl Kendrick studied bacteriology in university and was recruited by the Michigan Department of Health in 1920.  It was there that she met fellow bacteriologist Grace Eldering.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:

❌ ③ ran away(도망쳤다): 문맥과 맞지 않음
❌ ④ fell apart(무너졌다): 두 과학자의 등장이라는 긍정적 전환과 반대
